title: Part 1, Chapter 48
paragraphs: In which the canon continues on the subject of books of chivalry, with other matters worthy of his wit

"You are quite right, señor canon," said the curate; "and for that reason those who have so far written books of this sort deserve all the more censure for writing without paying any attention to good taste or the rules of art — by which they might have guided themselves and become as famous in prose as the two princes of Greek and Latin poetry are in verse."

"For my part," said the canon, "I was once tempted to write a book of chivalry in which all the points I've mentioned were to be observed; and if I must confess the truth, I have more than a hundred pages written. To test whether it lived up to my own opinion of it, I showed them to people who were fond of this kind of reading — to learned and intelligent men as well as to ignorant people who care for nothing but the pleasure of listening to nonsense — and from all of them I got flattering approval. Nevertheless I went no farther with it, both because it seemed to me an occupation inconsistent with my profession and because I saw that the fools are more numerous than the wise; and though it's better to be praised by the wise few than applauded by the foolish many, I have no wish to submit myself to the stupid judgment of the silly public, to whom the reading of such books falls for the most part.

"But what most made me hold my hand and even give up the idea of finishing it was an argument I put to myself drawn from the plays performed nowadays. It went like this: if those now in vogue — both the pure inventions and those founded on history — are, all or most of them, downright nonsense and things with neither head nor tail; and yet the public listens to them with delight and proclaims them perfect when they're far from it; and if the authors who write them and the players who act them say that this is what they must be, because the public wants this and nothing else; and that those who follow the rules and work out a plot according to the laws of art will only find some half-dozen intelligent people to understand them, while everyone else remains blind to the merit of their composition; and that for themselves it's better to get bread from the many than praise from the few — well then, my book will fare the same way, after I have scorched my eyebrows trying to observe the principles I've mentioned, and I shall be 'the tailor of the corner.' Though I've sometimes tried to convince actors they're mistaken in the opinion they've adopted, and that they would draw bigger audiences and earn more credit by producing plays that observe the rules of art rather than absurd ones, they are so thoroughly wedded to their own view that no argument or evidence can wean them from it.

"I remember saying one day to one of these obstinate fellows, 'Tell me, don't you remember that a few years ago there were three tragedies acted in Spain, written by a famous poet of these kingdoms, which were such that they filled all who heard them with admiration, delight, and interest — the ignorant as well as the wise, the masses as well as the higher orders — and brought in more money to the performers, these three alone, than thirty of the best produced since?'
"'No doubt,' replied the actor in question, 'you mean the "Isabella," the "Phyllis," and the "Alexandra."'

"'Those are the ones I mean,' I said; 'and see whether they didn't observe the principles of art, and whether, by observing them, they failed to show their superiority and please everyone. So the fault doesn't lie with the public that insists on nonsense, but with those who don't know how to produce anything else. "The Ingratitude Revenged" was not nonsense, nor was there any in "The Numantia," nor any to be found in "The Merchant Lover," nor yet in "The Friendly Fair Foe," nor in some others that have been written by certain gifted poets — to their own fame and renown and to the profit of those who brought them out.' I added a few more remarks to these, which I think left him rather dumbfounded but not so satisfied or convinced that I could disabuse him of his error."

"You've touched on a subject, señor canon," observed the curate, "that has awoken an old grievance of mine against the plays now in vogue — as strong as the one I bear against the books of chivalry. The drama, according to Tully, should be the mirror of human life, the model of manners, and the image of the truth; but those put on these days are mirrors of nonsense, models of folly, and images of lewdness. For what greater nonsense can there be on this subject than for an infant to appear in swaddling clothes in the first scene of the first act, and in the second a grown-up bearded man? Or what greater absurdity than putting before us an old man as a swashbuckler, a young man as a coward, a lackey using fine language, a page giving sage advice, a king moonlighting as a porter, or a princess as a kitchen-maid? And what shall I say of their concern for the time in which the action they represent could conceivably take place — except that I've seen a play where the first act began in Europe, the second in Asia, the third ended in Africa, and no doubt, had it had four acts, the fourth would have ended in America, so it would have been laid in all four quarters of the globe? And if truth to life is the main thing the drama should keep in view, how can any average understanding be satisfied when the action is supposed to pass in the time of King Pepin or Charlemagne, and the principal character in it is the Emperor Heraclius, who entered Jerusalem with the cross and won the Holy Sepulchre, like Godfrey of Bouillon — there being countless years between the two? Or, if the play is based on fiction, historical facts are introduced, or bits of what happened to different people at different times are mixed up with it, all with no semblance of probability but with obvious errors that from every point of view are inexcusable? And the worst of it is, there are ignorant people who say this is perfection and that anything beyond it is mere affectation. And then if we turn to sacred dramas — what miracles they invent in them! What apocryphal, ill-devised incidents, attributing to one saint the miracles of another! Even in secular plays they venture to introduce miracles without any reason or purpose except that they think some such miracle, or transformation as they call it, will go down well with the dim-witted and draw them to the play. All this tends to the prejudice of the truth and the corruption of history — indeed, to the disgrace of Spanish wit, for foreigners who scrupulously observe the laws of the drama look on us as barbarous and ignorant when they see the absurdity and nonsense of the plays we produce. Nor is it a sufficient excuse to say that the chief object well-ordered governments have in view when they permit public plays is to entertain the people with some harmless amusement now and then and keep them clear of the evil humours that idleness tends to breed, and that, as this may be achieved by any sort of play, good or bad, there's no need to lay down laws or bind those who write or act them to make them as they ought to be — since, as I say, the object sought may be achieved by any sort. To which I'd reply that the same end would be, beyond all comparison, better attained by good plays than by those that aren't, for after listening to an artistic and well-constructed play the hearer will come away enlivened by the jokes, instructed by the serious parts, full of admiration at the incidents, his wits sharpened by the arguments, warned by the deceptions, all the wiser for the examples, inflamed against vice, and in love with virtue; for in all these ways a good play will stir the mind of any hearer, however boorish or dull. And of all impossibilities the greatest is that a play endowed with all these qualities should not entertain, satisfy, and please much more than one wanting in them — like most of those commonly acted now. Nor are the poets who write them to be blamed; for some of them are perfectly aware of their faults and know what they should do, but since plays have become a saleable commodity, they say — and truly — that actors won't buy them unless they're after this fashion, so the poet tries to adapt to the requirements of the actor who's going to pay him. The proof can be seen in the countless plays a most fertile wit of these kingdoms has written, with such brilliance, such grace and gaiety, such polished versification, such choice language, such profound reflections — in a word, so rich in eloquence and elevation of style — that he has filled the world with his fame; and yet, because of his desire to suit the actors' taste, they haven't all, as some of them have, come as near perfection as they ought. Others write plays so carelessly that, after they've been acted, the actors have to flee and go into hiding for fear of being punished (as they often have been) for having acted something offensive to some king or other, or insulting to some noble family. All these evils, and many more I'm passing over, would be removed if at the capital there were some intelligent and sensible person to examine all plays before they were acted — not only those produced in the capital itself, but all that were meant to be acted in Spain — without whose approval, seal, and signature no local magistracy should allow any play to be performed. In that case actors would take care to send their plays to the capital, and could act them in safety; and those who write them would be more careful and take more pains with their work, knowing they would have to submit it to the strict examination of someone who understood the matter. So good plays would be produced, and the objects they aim at happily attained: the amusement of the people, the credit of Spanish wit, the interest and safety of the actors, and the saving of trouble in inflicting punishment on them. And if the same or some other person were authorised to examine the newly written books of chivalry, no doubt some would appear with all the perfections you've described, enriching our language with the gracious and precious treasure of eloquence, and driving the old books into obscurity before the light of the new ones, which would come out for the harmless entertainment not only of the idle but of the very busiest; for the bow cannot always be bent, nor can weak human nature exist without some lawful amusement."

The canon and the curate had gone this far with their conversation when the barber came up and joined them, saying to the curate, "This is the spot, señor licentiate, I said was a good one for fresh and plentiful pasture for the oxen while we take our noontide rest."

"So it seems," the curate replied, and he told the canon what he was planning to do. The canon, too, decided to halt with them, drawn by the look of the fair valley before them; and to enjoy it as well as the curate's conversation — for he had taken a liking to him — and to learn more about Don Quixote's doings, he directed some of his servants to ride on to the inn, which was not far off, and fetch whatever food there might be for the whole party, since he intended to rest for the afternoon where they were. One of his servants replied that the sumpter mule, which by now should have reached the inn, was carrying enough provisions to make it unnecessary to get anything from the inn except barley.
"In that case," said the canon, "take all the beasts there and bring the sumpter mule back."

While this was going on, Sancho, seeing he could speak to his master without the curate and the barber, of whom he was suspicious, being present all the time, came up to the cage in which Don Quixote sat and said, "Señor, to ease my conscience I want to tell you the truth about your enchantment, which is that these two men with their faces covered are the curate of our village and the barber. I suspect they've hit on this plan of carrying you off out of pure envy, because your worship surpasses them in doing famous deeds. And if that's the truth, it follows you are not enchanted but hoodwinked and made a fool of. And to prove this I want to ask you one thing; if you answer me as I believe you will, you'll be able to put your finger on the trick and see that you're not enchanted but out of your wits."

"Ask whatever you like, Sancho my son," Don Quixote returned, "and I will satisfy you and answer all you ask. As for what you say — that those accompanying us yonder are the curate and the barber, our neighbours and acquaintances — it is very possible they may seem to be those very people; but that they really and truly are so, don't believe it on any account. What you must believe and think is that if they look like them, as you say, it must be that those who have enchanted me have taken this shape and likeness; for enchanters can easily take any form they choose, and they may have taken those of our friends in order to make you think as you do, and lead you into a labyrinth of fancies from which you would not escape even if you had the thread of Theseus. They may also have done it to make me uncertain in my mind, unable to guess where this evil comes from. For if on the one hand you tell me the barber and curate of our village are here with us, and on the other I find myself shut up in a cage, knowing in my heart that no power on earth, short of the supernatural, could have shut me in, what would you have me say or think, except that my enchantment is of a kind that surpasses anything I have ever read of in all the histories that deal with enchanted knights-errant? So you may set your mind at rest about the idea that they are what you say, for they are as much that as I am a Turk. But as for what you want to ask me — ask away, and I'll answer, even if you have to keep asking questions from now till tomorrow morning."

"Our Lady help me!" said Sancho, raising his voice. "Is it possible your worship is so thick of skull and so short of brains that you can't see what I say is the simple truth, and that malice has more to do with your imprisonment and misfortune than enchantment? Since that's how things are, I'll prove plainly to you that you are not enchanted. Now tell me, so God may deliver you from this affliction, and so you may find yourself when you least expect it in the arms of my lady Dulcinea —"
"Stop conjuring me," said Don Quixote, "and ask what you want to know; I've already told you I'll answer as precisely as possible."

"That's what I want," said Sancho, "and what I'd like to know, and have you tell me, without adding or leaving anything out, but telling the whole truth as one expects it to be told, and as it is told, by all who profess arms, as your worship does, under the title of knights-errant —"
"I tell you I won't lie in any particular," said Don Quixote; "finish your question, for in truth you wear me out with all these vows, demands, and precautions, Sancho."

"Well, I rely on my master's goodness and truthfulness," said Sancho; "and so, because it bears on what we're talking about, I would ask, speaking with all reverence, whether since your worship has been shut up and, as you think, enchanted in this cage, you've felt any desire or inclination to go anywhere, as the saying is?"
"I don't understand 'going anywhere,'" said Don Quixote; "explain yourself more clearly, Sancho, if you want me to give a straight answer."

"Is it possible," said Sancho, "that your worship doesn't understand 'going anywhere'? Why, schoolboys know that from the time they were babies. Well then, I mean — have you had any desire to do what cannot be avoided?"
"Ah, now I understand you, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Yes, often, and right at this minute. Get me out of this fix, or things won't end well."
